prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: I keep my round-1 configuration unchanged: B027 alone, credited to Katori and Ye. After the full exchange my reasons are narrower and firmer than they were. The achievement is bounded and has a concrete before and after: the magic-wavelength condition lets a large ensemble of neutral atoms be held in a lattice without Doppler, recoil or differential light shifts, and the Ye group's operation of spin-polarised Fermi gases showed that the same arrangement can reach the 1e-18 regime and be used to probe many-body and relativistic effects. Independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) reproduce this performance, so neither confirmation nor maturity is in doubt. Six of eight members now name the same configuration, but I do not rely on that count; what persuades me is that the members who weigh the alternatives most carefully (Danielsson, Kroll, Lindroth) reach it through an attribution argument I can check myself, namely that two names map onto the originating concept and its realisation at extreme performance. On the chair's question about the redefinition of the second, I regard it as irrelevant to the physics and not a reason to wait: the committee honours an invention whose performance has been established independently, not a decision of the metrology bodies. A citation that names the optical lattice clock itself, and not optical clocks or precision spectroscopy in general, makes that separation from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 single-ion prize explicit.
statement.case_against: The overlap argument is the strongest one against me and I do not think it can be fully dismissed. Frequency combs (2005) and control of single quantum systems (2012) already honoured neighbouring pillars of optical metrology, and laser cooling was recognised in 1997. My answer is that the magic-wavelength lattice is a separate idea, not a refinement of ion-trap or comb technology, but a reasonable colleague can still judge the increment to be one of degree. Second, the credit leaves out ion-clock pioneers, other early Sr and Yb lattice groups and ultrastable-laser developers; a narrow citation reduces this problem but does not remove it. Third, the largest consequences (varying constants, dark-matter searches, geodesy, the new second) are still partly prospective. Finally, I should state plainly that I moved from B002, which I still consider the deeper conceptual contribution, and that my preference is therefore an argument from clean attribution and independent confirmation rather than from conceptual depth. If the committee were to find that B027 is mostly an extension of work already honoured, then B057 is the configuration I would turn to, with the attribution cost that I describe below.

responses.point: Olsson, who ranks B053 first, states that the clock overlaps strongly with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and that Ye's contribution is partly the pushing of accuracy rather than a distinct concept, while saying she would not insist on aberration correction if the committee finds the clock or topological candidates stronger.
responses.response: I take the overlap point seriously, and it is the argument that most nearly moves me. But I do not think it separates Katori from Ye the way she suggests: the many-body, spin-polarised Fermi-gas operation of a lattice clock, and the demonstration that systematic shifts of a many-atom lattice could be brought to 1e-18, are not merely an improvement of accuracy but the demonstration that the concept works at all at that level. I also respect her candour about B053; as an enabling instrument with Krivanek outside a three-name cap, it faces the same attribution difficulty that I use against other candidates, so I keep it out of my alternatives.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B057 and argues that a citation built on the Z2 classification and the observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe does not depend on who first proposed HgTe as the platform, and that fifteen years of independent confirmation make the case mature.
responses.response: His maturity argument is correct, and I agree that B057 is the principal rival to B027. My difficulty is with the claim that the citation can be drawn around the Z2 classification and the HgTe observation while the HgTe proposal itself (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) is not credited: the experiment was built on that proposal, so the citation would honour the result and leave out the people who told the experimentalists where to look. With the 2016 prize on topological phases already given, I think that credit problem is real and cannot be repaired by wording; I would take B057 as my second configuration, but not as my first.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved from IceCube to B027, but states that B041 opens a new observational window and is the larger discovery, and that he would hesitate to honour a theory such as B002 whose specific predictions are less well tested than its qualitative picture.
responses.response: I accept his criticism of B002 and have not tried to rescue it; the Toner-Tu exponents are tested less well than the existence of collective motion, and priority between the Vicsek and Toner-Tu strands is for different kinds of result, which is why B002 stays only as a final alternative. On B041 I agree that it is a discovery of the first rank, and I would not oppose it if the committee could write a fair credit for a very large collaboration with an AMANDA predecessor; since no member has found such a wording, I do not move it above B027, and his question about deference to astroparticle colleagues on whether Halzen and Karle are the decisive pair seems to me to answer itself in his own disclosure of field proximity.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B027 first with a citation tied to the 10^-18 level, accepts that the overlap with 2005 and 2012 cannot be fully dismissed, and judges the unresolved HgTe credit to be the deciding difference between B027 and B057.
responses.response: I agree that the HgTe credit is the deciding point, and I would add that it is the same kind of argument in both directions: for B027 it is a strength of the credit, and for B057 a weakness of it, which is a fair basis for an ordering and not a claim that the clock is the greater science. Where I differ slightly is on the wording of his citation. Putting the 10^-18 level into the citation ties the prize to a number that other groups will go on improving, so I prefer a citation that names the invention only.

responses.point: Johansson, in her answer to my own B002 case, argues that direct quantitative confirmation of the Toner-Tu exponents is thinner than the qualitative confirmation, and that the Vicsek and Toner-Tu strands would be credited for different kinds of results, so she does not rank it.
responses.response: She is right, and I concede it in full. I recall the experimental status from memory, and the existing tests of the exponents in simulations and in a few experimental systems do not amount to the systematic quantitative confirmation I would want before the committee honours a scaling theory. That is why I moved to B027, and why I keep B002 only as a last alternative, to be used only if the committee could be convinced that the theory had matured. Her own conflict disclosure on B036 also seems to me correct and I agree that it should reduce the weight of that ballot.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B027 first and says that the citation can be written to exclude ion clocks and comb technology, but also that a prize could be read as anticipating a metrological decision, and that B057 is arguably overdue after 2016.
responses.response: I agree that the citation can be written to exclude ion clocks and comb technology and I would hold to that, since otherwise the claims of the ion-clock pioneers become hard to refuse. I still disagree with the idea that B057 is overdue. Whether a field has waited is an argument from timing, and not an argument about credit, and with the three-name cap it is the credit that is unresolved; this is the position I put to her in round 1 and nothing in the later statements has changed it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the optical lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb prize, the 2012 single-quantum-system prize and the laser-cooling prizes; I judge it distinct but cannot show this beyond argument.
Whether ion-clock pioneers, early Sr and Yb lattice groups or ultrastable-laser developers have a claim that a two-name credit cannot reflect; I rely on a narrow citation to manage it.
Whether the largest consequences of the clock (a new definition of the second, varying constants, dark-matter searches) will be realised as supporters expect.
My recollection of the experimental status of the Toner-Tu exponents and of priority dates in the HgTe literature comes from memory and has not been verified in this stage.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile: none of my documented co-authors or institutions (Fulde, Gustavsson, Wilkinson, Einarsson, Candelier, Pumir, Meibohm; Max Planck institutes, Oxford, Freiburg, Gothenburg) includes Katori, Ye or any other credited name on the shortlist. I repeat my disclosure of intellectual proximity, not a personal tie, to active matter (B002) and stochastic processes, which is why my preference for B027 rests on attribution and independent confirmation and not on my own field. I do not see a need for my own recusal, and I note that Olsson, Johansson and Lindroth have each disclosed proximity to B053, B036 and B027 respectively, which I think should be weighed and not treated as a bar to their votes.
